impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to administering a genus of antibodies requires the same breadth-of-genus analysis applied to composition claims, particularly after Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against an enablement challenge. The dissent argued the panel's holding undermines Amgen v. Sanofi by sustaining overly broad method claims covering a genus of antibodies, creating confusion about enablement standards for method versus composition claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of biologics retain stronger protection, as the Federal Circuit declined to extend the more demanding Amgen enablement analysis to method claims where any member of the genus achieves the claimed function.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and generic/biosimilar companies face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, as this ruling permits patent owners to claim entire genera of antibodies in method claims without demonstrating enablement across the full scope, potentially increasing licensing costs and delaying market entry.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee such that it constituted a virtual assignment, and whether the licensee's shift from active commercialization to enforcement-only activities triggered a termination clause in the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M did not automatically terminate when the licensee shifted to enforcement activities, and that the license conveyed all substantial rights in the patents, allowing the licensee to sue without joining the patent owner. The court found A&M was not a necessary party under Rule 19(a).
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarification that shifting business operations to enforcement does not automatically terminate a license, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue independently without joining the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on standing and joinder arguments, and universities and other patent owners may find it harder to regain control over enforcement when licensees pivot solely to litigation-based business models.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and in its judgment on damages for trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract under the Defend Trade Secrets Act and Michigan law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award and reinstated the original jury verdict, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation of Ford's configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the court's instruction that district courts must more carefully consider alternative damages methodologies before excluding expert testimony, and the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award protects plaintiffs' damages recoveries.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop software in-house after licensing third-party technology face continued exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims, and the remand for reconsideration of additional damages models may increase potential liability for misappropriating parties.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results without specifying which method defines the claimed range.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of the '287 patent directed to waterproof breathable membranes are invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could be measured using different methods (upright, inverted, or Mocon) yielding different results, and the patent failed to inform skilled artisans with reasonable certainty which method defined the claimed range.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and performance-textile industries gain a strong defense when patent claims rely on performance metrics measurable by multiple standardized methods that yield divergent results without specifying the applicable test.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders claiming performance ranges must ensure their specifications clearly identify the measurement methodology, or risk invalidation; this decision increases drafting burdens for patents in industries where multiple standardized testing protocols exist.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and how to assess eligibility when claims involve mathematical optimization applied to specific communication system hardware.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on eligibility, vacating summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings. The decision provides guidance on when claims integrating mathematical concepts into communication system implementations satisfy the Alice/Mayo framework.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies with patents claiming specific hardware implementations of mathematically-optimized communication techniques benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for the '509 and '922 patent claims, reinforcing that claims tied to concrete technical improvements in communication systems can survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies asserting broadly-claimed signal processing patents face increased § 101 vulnerability, as the court vacated eligibility for claims that did not sufficiently tie the mathematical optimization to specific technical implementations, requiring remand and potential invalidity findings.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for indefiniteness or lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement. The court held that although the claim terms were sufficiently definite, the patent failed to enable the full scope of the claimed invention, particularly the impedance-matching coupler for wireless transmission over air.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants gain a confirmed pathway to invalidate patents on enablement grounds even where indefiniteness challenges fail, providing a robust alternative invalidity defense for patents claiming broad physical phenomena.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims covering fundamental physical concepts face heightened enablement scrutiny, as the Federal Circuit showed willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached by the district court.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract dispute regarding interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether the dispute is a state law contract interpretation issue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over T-Mobile's appeal from a summary judgment enforcing a settlement agreement's contingent payment provision, finding the dispute was fundamentally about contract interpretation under Texas law rather than patent law. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit, emphasizing that interpreting the phrase 'survives the EPR' did not necessarily require resolution of a substantial patent question.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties drafting patent settlement agreements receive important guidance on how ambiguous contingent payment clauses will be treated jurisdictionally, and defendants may benefit from having contract disputes heard in regional circuits rather than the patent-specialized Federal Circuit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies entering patent settlement agreements face uncertainty about which appellate court will interpret their agreements, potentially increasing litigation costs and forum-shopping risks when settlement terms reference patent proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient reasoning when denying a motion for attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 and a related patent was invalidated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of Pen-Tech's motion for sanctions and attorneys' fees, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that filed suit despite PTO rejections of related applications under § 101 and a sister court's invalidation of a related patent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers who prevail on § 101 grounds gain stronger support for fee-shifting motions, as the Federal Circuit signals that courts must carefully analyze whether pursuing litigation in the face of prior § 101 rejections of related applications constitutes exceptional case conduct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when filing infringement suits where related applications have been rejected under § 101, requiring more careful pre-suit evaluation of claim viability.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to oil and gas casing tools, and whether the jury's infringement and validity findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment of infringement and damages related to a patent on casing flotation devices used in oil and gas wellbore operations, finding errors in claim construction of the term 'internal diameter.' The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the corrected construction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas equipment industry benefit from stricter claim construction analysis, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted patent claims on remand.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy sector face the risk of having favorable jury verdicts vacated based on claim construction errors, requiring retrial and potentially narrower claim scope on remand.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims to crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salt forms satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification discloses the salt in both crystalline and amorphous forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of Exelixis's malate salt patents have adequate written description, upholding patent protection for the cabozantinib (L)-malate salt used in the cancer drug Cabometyx®. The decision supports Exelixis's ability to block generic entry through 2030.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from confirmation that claims to specific crystalline salt forms satisfy written description when the specification adequately distinguishes crystalline from amorphous forms, reinforcing protection for blockbuster oncology drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the affirmance of these patents extends exclusivity and delays lower-cost alternatives for cancer patients.

impacts.caseName: Traxcell Technologies, LLC v. Cellco Partnership
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court other than the one that entered an attorneys' fees award under 35 U.S.C. § 285 has jurisdiction over an independent action under Rule 60(d)(1) seeking to void that fee judgment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Western District of Texas's judgment denying Traxcell's independent action to void an attorneys' fees award entered by the Eastern District of Texas, holding that the Western District lacked jurisdiction over the independent action. The court remanded with instructions to dismiss, reinforcing that challenges to patent fee awards must be brought before the court that entered the judgment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Fee-award holders benefit from the ruling that losing parties cannot forum-shop by filing independent actions in different districts to challenge § 285 fee judgments, providing greater finality to fee awards in patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties seeking to challenge patent fee awards have limited avenues for relief, as the Federal Circuit confirmed that independent actions to void such judgments cannot be pursued in courts other than the one that entered the original fee order.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court that dismisses a patent case for improper venue may also reach the merits of a § 101 patent eligibility challenge and dismiss on that additional ground.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal of a patent infringement case on both improper venue and § 101 ineligibility grounds. The court held that the district court did not err in addressing the merits of the patent eligibility challenge even after finding venue was improper, allowing the § 101 dismissal to stand alongside the venue dismissal.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based dismissals (such as § 101 ineligibility) even when venue is improper, potentially providing broader preclusive effect and deterring refiling in other venues.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face the risk that a venue challenge will not merely result in transfer or dismissal without prejudice, but may instead lead to a binding merits ruling on patent eligibility that forecloses reassertion of the same claims elsewhere.
